text: Given an integer array nums, return true if any value appears at least twice, and false if every element is distinct.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I only need a yes or no on whether any duplicate exists, not which value, and not how many times. And values can be negative, any thirty-two-bit int? Are there any constraints on the input size?
Correct — just existence. Up to ten to the fifth elements, values anywhere in the int range.

Got it. Up to a hundred thousand elements, so I want better than quadratic. Let me run through the example. One, two, three, one is true, because the one repeats. One, two, three, four is false — all distinct.

Let me think about the options. A naive approach would be a double loop comparing every pair. That's quadratic, which times out at ten to the fifth. Sorting first puts equal values next to each other, so one pass finds a duplicate in n log n time, but it reorders the input. This problem reminds me of the classic seen-set pattern: remember every value I've passed, and the moment I'm about to record one that's already in the set, that's a duplicate. That's linear time. Since we only need existence, a set is enough — no need for counts.

Here's the plan. One: start with an empty hash set called seen. Two: for each value, check first — if it's already in seen, return true right away. Three: otherwise insert it, and if the scan finishes, return false. One thing worth flagging — the order matters: check before insert. If I inserted first, every element would immediately find itself, and I'd always return true. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. It's one loop over the array with an unordered set called seen. For each element, I ask the set whether it already holds the value; if so, I return true on the spot, and otherwise I insert it for later elements to compare against. If the loop ends, everything was distinct, so I return false. The line that's easy to get wrong is the order of count and insert — count must come first, so I'm asking about earlier elements, not the one I just added. Count returns zero or one for a set, so it reads as a clean boolean. That's average linear time and linear space.
You said linear — is that guaranteed?

It's amortized, on average. Each lookup and insert is constant time on average, but a hash table occasionally rehashes — reallocating buckets and moving everything, a linear event — and that cost spreads out to constant per operation. The theoretical worst case is linear per operation if every key collides into one bucket, making the whole thing quadratic, but with a decent hash that essentially never happens. So: linear on average overall, quadratic in the worst case under pathological collisions.

Let's dry-run the code on one, two, three, one — expected true. The first three values are all new, so they just go into the set. The row that matters is index three: the value one is already in seen, so I return true right there, without touching anything after it. That matches. Corner cases: one, two, three, four scans all four and returns false. A single element returns false, since there's nothing to pair it with. Negative values, like minus one, minus one, hash like any other int and return true. And if every value is the same, I return true as early as index one.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear on average, space is linear, and it exits early on the first duplicate. Oh, one more thing — if you constrained me to constant extra space, I'd sort and check adjacent equals: n log n time, constant space, at the cost of reordering the input. That's the classic time-space trade. The hash spends linear memory to save time; the sort spends time to save memory. And if the ask changed to how many times each value repeats, I'd switch the set to a map of counts and lose the early exit, since counting needs the full scan.
Clean. You picked the right structure for existence-only, got the check-before-insert ordering, and were precise about amortized versus worst case. Nice warm-up pass.
